sourceBody: Before you dig anything, it helps to know how the decisions get made.
This module is the foundation for everything else in the course. Three ethics, a set of design principles, and one simple way to organise your land.
None of it needs money. All of it changes where you put things, and how far you walk every day.
Think about your own plot. Which part of it do you visit most often?
recommendedBody: Musi ni sa athu u gwa, zwi a thusa u ḓivha uri tsheo dzi dzhiiwa hani.
Modulu uyu ndi mutheo wa zwoṱhe zwiṅwe kha ngudo ino. Three ethics, a set of design principles, na nḓila nthihi yo leluwaho ya u dzudzanya land yaṋu.
A zwi ṱoḓi tshelede. Zwoṱhe zwi shandula hune na vhea zwithu, na uri ni tshimbila vhukale vhu ngafhani ḓuvha ḽiṅwe na ḽiṅwe.
Humbulani nga ha tsimu yaṋu. Ndi tshipiḓa tshifhio tshine na tshi dalela lunzhi?

sourceBody: A good design saves work before you pick up a spade.
Most of the effort on a smallholding is not planting or harvesting. It is walking, carrying and fixing what was put in the wrong place.
Permaculture is a way of deciding where things go, so the land works with you instead of against you.
Think of one job on your farm that takes longer than it should. Where does the time actually go?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Ndi ngani hezwi zwi zwa ndeme
recommendedBody: Design yavhuḓi i fhungudza mushumo ni sa athu u fara spade.
Mushumo munzhi kha bulasi ḽiṱuku a si wa u zwala kana u kaṋa. Ndi wa u tshimbila, u hwala na u lugisa zwe zwa vhewa fhethu hu songo teaho.
Permaculture ndi nḓila ya u dzhia tsheo ya hune zwithu zwa tea u vha hone, uri mavu a shume na inwi, hu si u ni thivhela.
Humbulani nga mushumo muthihi bulasini yaṋu une wa dzhia tshifhinga tshilapfu u fhira tshine tsha ṱoḓea. Tshifhinga tshi khou ya ngafhi zwa vhukuma?

sourceBody: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things.
Name the three ethics, and use them to settle a decision that has no obvious answer.
Name the design principles that matter most on your land, and say why.
Sketch your zones and your sectors on one sheet of paper.
That sketch is the skeleton of every plan you make after this.
recommendedBody: Musi modzhulu uyu wo no fhela, ni ḓo kona u ita zwithu zwiraru.
Bulani the three ethics, ni dzi shumise u dzhia tsheo ine ya si vhe na phindulo i vhonalaho.
Bulani design principles dzi re dza ndeme nga maanḓa kha land yaṋu, ni bule na uri ndi ngani.
Olani zones na sectors dzaṋu kha bammbiri ḽithihi.
Tshifanyiso itsho ndi mutheo wa pulane iṅwe na iṅwe ine na ḓo i ita nga murahu ha izwi.

sourceBody: The first ethic is Earth Care.
It means treating soil, water, plants and animals as living systems to protect, not resources to use up.
A system you use up stops paying you. A system you protect keeps paying you.
Look at one patch of bare soil on your land. Is anything protecting it right now?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: U Ṱhogomela Mavu na Mupo (Earth Care)
recommendedBody: Mulayo wa vhuḓifari wa u thoma ndi U Ṱhogomela Mavu na Mupo (Earth Care).
Zwi amba u dzhia mavu, maḓi, zwimela na zwipuka sa “living systems to protect, not resources to use up.”
System ine na shumisa na fhedza i a ima: “stops paying you.” System ine na tsireledza i bvela phanda: “keeps paying you.”
Sedzani tshipiḓa tshithihi tsha mavu a songo tibedzwaho tsimuni yaṋu. Hu na tshithu tshine tsha khou tsireledza mavu eneo zwino?

sourceBody: The second ethic is People Care.
Your family's needs come first, then your community's.
A farmer who sells every egg and every vegetable, and keeps nothing back for the family table, is skipping People Care.
The farm is meant to feed the household that runs it.
What comes off your land that your own family never eats?
recommendedBody: Mulayo wa vhuḓifari wa vhuvhili ndi U Ṱhogomela Vhathu (People Care).
Ṱhoḓea dza muṱa waṋu dzi ḓa u thoma, nga murahu hu tevhela dza tshitshavha tsha haṋu.
Murimi ane a rengisa makumba oṱhe na miroho yoṱhe, a si vhee na tshithu tsha uḽa ha muṱa, ha tevheli People Care.
Bulasi ḽo itelwa u ṋea zwiḽiwa muṱa une wa ḽi shumisa.
Ndi mini zwine zwa bva shangoni ḽaṋu zwine muṱa waṋu wa sa vhuye wa zwiḽa?

sourceBody: The third ethic is Fair Share.
Take only what you need, and return the surplus to the system — seeds, food, water, knowledge.
A farmer who sells all his surplus mielies and keeps nothing back for compost or for seed is breaking this one. Nothing goes back.
A community that fences off a shared spring is breaking it too.
What does your land get back from you each season?
recommendedBody: Mulayo wa vhuḓifari wa vhuraru ndi U Kovhelana ho Fanelaho (Fair Share).
Dzhiani fhedzi zwine na zwi ṱoḓa, nahone return the surplus to the system — mbeu, zwiḽiwa, maḓi, nḓivho.
Mulimi ane a rengisa mielies dzawe dzoṱhe dza surplus, a si vhulunge na tshithu tsha compost kana mbeu, u khou pfuka uyu mulayo. A hu na tshithu tshi vhuyelelaho.
Tshitshavha tshi vhofhaho tsime ḽine ḽa shumiswa nga vhoṱhe nga fence tshi khou pfuka Fair Share na tshone.
Land yaṋu i wana mini kha inwi kha khalaṅwaha iṅwe na iṅwe?

sourceBody: A borehole serves your household. Neighbours ask for water too.

First find out if sharing is allowed. Check whether the borehole can serve all users without taking too much. If sharing is allowed and there is enough water, agree how to share fairly and keep watching the water level. People Care and Fair Share guide the agreement. Earth Care means protecting the source. Watching the level alone does not make extra use safe or allowed.
Who could help you check the rules and the water supply?
recommendedBody: A borehole i shumela muṱa waṋu. Vhahura vha khou humbela maḓi na vhone.

Thomani nga u wana arali u kovhelana ho tendelwa. Check whether the borehole can serve all users without taking too much. Arali u kovhelana ho tendelwa nahone hu na maḓi o eḓanaho, tendelanani uri ni kovhelane nga ndinganyo ni dzule ni tshi sedza water level. People Care na Fair Share zwi livhisa u tendelana. Earth Care zwi amba u tsireledza the source. U sedza water level fhedzi a zwi ambi uri u shumisa maḓi o engedzeaho zwi safe kana zwo tendelwa.
Ndi nnyi ane a nga ni thusa u sedza milayo na water supply?

sourceBody: This is what the ethics are actually for.
A neighbour asks to graze cattle after a drought. A flood damages your swales. Nobody has written down the answer.
The ethics help you weigh the choices and explain your decision. Check the rules and ask permission where it is needed.
Build these three into how you think before you build anything on the ground.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Musi hu si na bugu ya milayo
recommendedBody: Hezwi ndi zwone zwine milayo ya vhuḓifari ya itelwa zwone.
Muhura u humbela u fulisa kholomo nga murahu ha gomelelo. A flood damages your swales. A hu na muthu o ṅwalaho phindulo.
Milayo ya vhuḓifari i ni thusa u pima khetho na u ṱalutshedza tsheo yaṋu. Ṱolani milayo nahone ni humbele thendelo hune zwa ṱoḓea hone.
Dzhiani ethics idzi tharu ni dzi ite tshipiḓa tsha nḓila ine na humbula ngayo, ni sa athu fhaṱa zwithu kha mavu.

sourceBody: David Holmgren set out twelve design principles in Essence of Permaculture. Bill Mollison and David Holmgren co-originated the permaculture concept.
You do not need all twelve to start. Three useful starting points for this lesson are: observe and interact, catch and store energy, and use edges and value the marginal.
We will take those three one at a time.
recommendedBody: David Holmgren o vhea milayo ya fumi-mbili ya nzudzanyo (twelve design principles) kha Essence of Permaculture. Bill Mollison na David Holmgren vho thoma muhumbulo wa permaculture vhothe.

A zwi ṱoḓi uri ni vhe na yoṱhe ya fumi-mbili u itela u thoma. Zwipiḓa zwiraru zwavhuḓi zwa u thoma ngudo ino ndi: u lavhelesa na u shumisana (observe and interact), u fara na u vhulunga maanḓa (catch and store energy), na u shumisa mikombero na u dzhiela nṱha zwipiḓa zwa thungo (use edges and value the marginal).
Ri ḓo dzhia hezwo zwiraru tshithihi nga tshithihi.

sourceBody: Watch your land through a full season before you commit to major earthworks.
One storm shows you one moment. A full wet season shows you the pattern — where water runs, where it pools, where it never reaches.

This helps you understand the site. It does not by itself show that a swale is suitable or safe to build. Before digging, check the soil, slope, drainage and a safe overflow route that will not cause erosion or send damaging water to neighbours. Ask a trained local adviser to assess the site.
Where does water leave your land? Do you actually know, or are you guessing?
recommendedBody: Sedzani land yaṋu through a full season before you commit to major earthworks.
One storm i sumbedza tshifhinga tshithihi. Full wet season i sumbedza pattern: hune maḓi a elela, hune a kuvhangana, na hune a sa swike hone.

Izwi zwi thusa uri ni pfesese site. Fhedzi izwi fhedzi a zwi sumbedzi uri swale yo tea kana yo safe u fhaṱiwa. Ni sa athu cela, sedzani soil, slope, drainage na safe overflow route ine ya sa ise kha erosion kana u rumela maḓi a tshinyadzaho kha vhahura. Humbelani trained local adviser uri a sedze site.
Maḓi a bva ngafhi kha land yaṋu? Ni a ḓivha zwa vhukuma, kana ni khou humbulela?

sourceBody: Harvest rain, sun and biomass before they leave your property.
Every one of those arrives free and leaves free. Water runs off, leaves blow away, sun falls on bare ground.
Compare the cost and work with the benefit on your own farm.
Name one thing that arrives on your land free and leaves again without being used.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Ni fare nahone ni vhulunge maanḓa
recommendedBody: Harvest rain, sun na biomass ni sa athu u zwi xedza kha property yaṋu.
Zwoṱhe izwi zwi swika mahala, zwa dovha zwa ṱuwa mahala. Maḓi a elela a tshi bva, maṱari a fhufha a tshi ṱuwa, ḓuvha ḽi wela kha mavu a songo fukedzwaho.
Vhambedzani the cost and work with the benefit kha bulasi yaṋu.
Bulani tshithu tshithihi tshine tsha swika kha mavu aṋu mahala tsha dovha tsha ṱuwa tshi songo shumiswa.

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Use Edges and Value the Marginal
sourceBody: The edge is where two things meet — a fence line or the strip beside a path.
These can be useful places to observe. Look at what already grows well along yours. That is the land telling you something.
Which edge on your plot is doing nothing at the moment?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Ni shumise mikano nahone ni dzhiele nṱha zwa magumoni
recommendedBody: The edge ndi hune zwithu zwivhili zwa ṱangana — a fence line or the strip beside a path.
Hezwi zwi nga vha fhethu hu vhuedzaho ha u sedza. Sedzani zwine zwa mela zwavhuḓi kha edge yaṋu. That is the land telling you something.
Ndi edge ifhio ya plot yaṋu ine zwa zwino ya si shume tshithu?

sourceBody: Use and value diversity. Hail injury to maize depends on the storm and the crop’s growth stage. This principle does not promise that a crop will survive every event.
Two others worth knowing: produce no waste, so scraps become compost and compost becomes soil. And use small and slow solutions — a bucket can irrigate a bed with no electricity at all.
What would one bad day cost you right now?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Ni shumise nahone ni dzhiele nṱha u fhambana
recommendedBody: Shumisani diversity ni i dzhiele nṱha. Hail injury to maize depends on the storm and the crop’s growth stage. Principle iyi a i fulufhedzisi uri crop i ḓo ponyoka kha tshiwo tshiṅwe na tshiṅwe.

Maṅwe maitele mavhili ane zwa vhuedza u a ḓivha ndi haya: produce no waste, so scraps become compost and compost becomes soil. And use small and slow solutions — bakete ḽi nga sheledza bed hu si na muḓagasi na luthihi.
Ḓuvha ḽithihi ḽivhi ḽi nga ni durisa mini zwino?

sourceBody: Put each element where it works for its neighbours.

A garden, fruit trees and a chicken run arranged so the chickens rotate through the beds after harvest is integration. Keep chickens away from crops being harvested for food. Fresh manure can carry germs. Ask an extension adviser how to manage the bed safely before edible crops return. The chickens can clean up pests and add fertility instead of sitting idle in a fixed pen.
The same three things, fenced apart, do only their own job.
Pick two or three principles that speak to your biggest problem and apply them hard. The rest become obvious as you go.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Ni ṱanganye nṱhani ha u fhambanya
recommendedBody: Vheani tshithu tshiṅwe na tshiṅwe (each element) fhethu hune tsha shumela zwi re tsini natsho (its neighbours).

A garden, miri ya mitshelo na chicken run zwi nga dzudzanywa uri khuhu dzi rotate through the beds after harvest; izwi ndi integration. Ni songo tendela khuhu dzi tshi swika kha crops dzine dza khou harvestiwa uri dzi ḽiwe. Fresh manure can carry germs. Vhudzisani extension adviser uri bed i langulwe hani safely, edible crops dzi sa athu dovha u hula. Khuhu dzi nga thusa u bvisa pests na u engedza fertility, nṱhani ha uri dzi dzule dzi sa shumi kha fixed pen.
Izwi zwithu zwiraru, zwo fhandekanywaho nga fence, zwi ita mushumo wa tshone tshithihi tshithihi fhedzi.
Khethani principles mbili kana tharu dzine dza amba na thaidzo yaṋu khulwane ni dzi shumise nga maanḓa. Dziṅwe dzi ḓo tou vha khagala musi ni tshi bvela phanḓa.

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Zones: Organising by How Often You Visit
sourceBody: Zones run from 0 to 5, and they are about your feet, not your fences.
Zone 0 is the house. In this example, Zone 1 is near the house and holds herbs and salad greens picked often.
Zone 2 is the main garden and the chicken run, visited once or twice a day. Zone 3 is the main field, visited weekly.
Zone 4 is semi-wild — fruit trees and fodder that need occasional attention. Zone 5 is left wild.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Zones: Organising by How Often You Visit
recommendedBody: Zones dzi bva kha 0 u ya kha 5, nahone ndi nga ha u tshimbila haṋu, hu si fences yaṋu.
Zone 0 ndi nḓu. Kha hei tsumbo, Zone 1 i tsini na nḓu nahone i na herbs and salad greens zwine na zwi kaṋa lunzhi.
Zone 2 ndi main garden na chicken run, ni zwi dalela luthihi kana luvhili nga ḓuvha. Zone 3 ndi main field, ni i dalela vhege iṅwe na iṅwe.
Zone 4 ndi semi-wild: miri ya mitshelo na fodder zwine zwa ṱoḓa ṱhogomelo nga zwiṅwe zwifhinga. Zone 5 i sala i wild.

sourceBody: Herbs you pick often are easier to tend near the house.
Put them far away, and the long walk may mean you miss a visit. The herbs may be neglected.
Think about the paths you walk each day.
What do you visit often that could be closer?
recommendedBody: Herbs dzine na dzi kaṋa lunzhi dzi a leluwa u dzi ṱhogomela dzi tsini na nḓu.
Arali na dzi vhea kule, lwendo lulapfu lu nga ita uri ni kundelwe u dzi dalela. Herbs dzi nga litshelelwa.
Humbulani nga nḓila dzine na tshimbila khadzo ḓuvha ḽiṅwe na ḽiṅwe.
Ndi zwifhio zwine na zwi dalela kanzhi zwine zwa nga vha tsini?

sourceBody: This is the point of the whole exercise.
Zones help organise space around your effort — the walking, the carrying and the checking that fills a real day.
The more often something needs you, the closer it lives. That can save walking and work over a season.
Stand at your kitchen door. What can you reach without thinking about it?
recommendedBody: Ndivho ya nyito yoṱhe ndi iyi.
Zones zwi thusa u dzudzanya fhethu u ya nga mushumo waṋu — u tshimbila, u hwala na u sedza zwine zwa ḓadza ḓuvha ḽa vhukuma.
Tshithu tshi ni ṱoḓaho lunzhi tshi dzula tsini na inwi. Zwenezwo zwi nga fhungudza u tshimbila na mushumo kha khalaṅwaha.
Imani muṋangoni wa khishini. Ndi zwifhio zwine na swikelela khazwo ni sa humbuli?

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Sectors: The Energies Arriving From Outside
sourceBody: Zones come from inside your land. Sectors come from outside it.
Sun, wind, rain, flood and fire all arrive across your boundary whether you plan for them or not.
Watch where strong wind comes from on your farm. Nearby weather-station records can help you check wind direction. Watch where rainwater enters and flows across your land.
Which direction does the weather that damages you come from?
recommendedBody: Zones dzi bva ngomu ha land yaṋu. Sectors dzi bva nnḓa ha yona.
Ḓuvha, muya, mvula, flood na mulilo zwi pfuka boundary yaṋu hu sa londwi arali ni tshi zwi pulanela kana hai.

Sedzani hune muya u re na maanḓa u bva hone kha bulasi yaṋu. Nearby weather-station records dzi nga ni thusa u sedza wind direction. Sedzani hune maḓi a mvula a dzhena hone na hune a elela hone kha mavu aṋu.
Mutsho une wa ni vhaisa u bva lufhio lurumbu?

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Watch: Shelter Between Wind and Crops
sourceBody: Look at this example. The wind comes from the north-west.
The trees and shrubs stand between that wind and the crops.
Some air passes through the windbreak. Other air moves over it or around its ends.
The shelter can reduce wind speed behind it. The design and care of the windbreak matter.
On your own site, observe the damaging winds before choosing where to plant. This picture is not a planting plan.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Ṱolisisani: Tsireledzo Vhukati Ha Muya Na Zwimela
recommendedBody: Sedzani uyu tsumbo. Muya u bva north-west.
Miri na shrubs dzi ima vhukati ha muya uyo na crops.
Muṅwe muya u fhira nga ngomu ha windbreak. Muṅwe u ya nṱha ha yone kana u mona na magumo ayo.
Shelter i nga fhungudza luvhilo lwa muya nga murahu hayo. Design na u ṱhogomela windbreak ndi zwa ndeme.
Kha site yaṋu, ṱhogomelani meya i tshinyadzaho ni sa athu khetha where to plant. Tshifanyiso itshi a si planting plan.

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Sketch It And You Have A Design
sourceBody: Draw your boundary. Mark the house. Draw the rings outward by how often you visit.
Then draw arrows in from outside for sun, wind, fire and water.
That sheet of paper is the skeleton of your design. Everything else in this course hangs on it.
It does not need to be neat. It needs to be true.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Zwi Olani Ndi Hone Ni Tshi Vha Na Nzudzanyo (Design)
recommendedBody: Olani boundary yaṋu. Maka nnḓu. Olani rings dzi tshi ya nnḓa u ya nga uri ni dalela hani lunzhi.
Nga murahu olani misevhe i tshi dzhena i tshi bva nnḓa u sumbedza ḓuvha, muya, mulilo na maḓi.
Bammbiri iḽi ndi mutheo wa pulane yaṋu. Zwiṅwe zwoṱhe kha ngudo iyi zwi fhaṱiwa khaḽo.
A zwi ṱoḓei uri zwi vhe zwo naka tshoṱhe. Zwi tea u vha ngoho.

sourceBody: Sketch your own zones and sectors on one sheet of paper.
Mark Zone 0 and Zone 1 first, then work outward as far as your land goes.
Add an arrow for each energy that arrives from outside, and label where it comes from.
Photograph the sketch.
recommendedBody: Olani own zones and sectors kha bammbiri ḽithihi.
Maka Zone 0 na Zone 1 u thome, ni bvele nga nnḓa u swika hune land yaṋu ya guma hone.
Engedzani musevhe muthihi kha energy iṅwe na iṅwe ine ya swika i tshi bva nnḓa, ni ṅwale hune ya bva hone.
Dzhiani photo ya sketch.

sourceBody: Walk out and check your sketch against the ground.
Stand at the kitchen door and count what is really in Zone 1 today.
Find one thing planted further away than how often you use it, and write down where it should move to.
Then ask one older neighbour which direction the worst wind comes from, and compare their answer with your arrow.
recommendedBody: Tshimbilani ni sedzani nyolo yaṋu ni tshi i vhambedza na ground ya vhukuma.
Imani munyangoni wa khishi ni vhale zwine zwa vha zwa vhukuma kha Zone 1 namusi.
Wanani tshithu tshithihi tsho ṱavhiwaho further away than how often you use it, ni ṅwale hune tsha tea u pfuluselwa hone.
Nga murahu ni humbele older neighbour muthihi uri a ni vhudze direction ine worst wind ya bva ngaḽo, ni vhambedze phindulo yawe na musevhe waṋu.

sourceBody: Before you dig anything, it helps to know how the decisions get made.
This module is the foundation for everything else in the course. Three ethics, a set of design principles, and one simple way to organise your land.
None of it needs money. All of it changes where you put things, and how far you walk every day.
Think about your own plot. Which part of it do you visit most often?
recommendedBody: U nga si cela, swi pfuna ku tiva leswaku swiboho swi endliwa hi ndlela yihi.
Modulu lowu i xisekelo xa swilo leswin’wana eka dyondzo leyi. Three ethics, a set of design principles, na ndlela yin’we yo olova yo hlela land ya wena.
A swi lavi mali. Hinkwaswu swi cinca laha u vekaka swilo kona ni leswaku u famba mpfhuka wo fika kwihi siku rin’wana ni rin’wana.
Ehleketa hi nsimu ya wena. Hi xihi xiphemu xa yona lexi u xi endzelaka ngopfu?

sourceBody: A good design saves work before you pick up a spade.
Most of the effort on a smallholding is not planting or harvesting. It is walking, carrying and fixing what was put in the wrong place.
Permaculture is a way of deciding where things go, so the land works with you instead of against you.
Think of one job on your farm that takes longer than it should. Where does the time actually go?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Ha yini leswi swi ri swa nkoka
recommendedBody: Dizayini leyinene yi hunguta ntirhokulu u nga si sungula ku cela.
Ntirho wo tala eka purasi leritsongo a hi ku byala kumbe ku tshovela. I ku famba, ku rhwala ni ku lulamisa leswi vekiweke endhawini leyi hoxeke.
Permaculture i ndlela yo teka swiboho hi laha swilo swi faneleke ku vekiwa kona, leswaku misava yi tirha na wena ku nga ri ku lwisana na wena.
Ehleketa hi ntirho wun'we epurasini ra wena lowu tekaka nkarhi wo tala ku nga ri na xilaveko. Nkarhi wolowo wu ya kwihi hakunene?

sourceBody: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things.
Name the three ethics, and use them to settle a decision that has no obvious answer.
Name the design principles that matter most on your land, and say why.
Sketch your zones and your sectors on one sheet of paper.
That sketch is the skeleton of every plan you make after this.
recommendedBody: Loko modulu lowu wu hela, u ta kota ku endla swilo swinharhu.
Boxa milawu ya mahanyelo yinharhu, u yi tirhisa ku endla xiboho lexi nga riki na nhlamulo leyi vonakaka hi ku olova.
Boxa design principles ta nkoka ngopfu eka land ya wena, u vula leswaku ha yini.
Dirowa zones na sectors ta wena eka phepha rin’we.
Xifaniso xexo hi xona xisekelo xa pulani yin'wana ni yin'wana leyi u nga ta yi endla endzhaku ka leswi.

sourceBody: The first ethic is Earth Care.
It means treating soil, water, plants and animals as living systems to protect, not resources to use up.
A system you use up stops paying you. A system you protect keeps paying you.
Look at one patch of bare soil on your land. Is anything protecting it right now?
recommendedBody: Nawu wo sungula wa mahanyelo i Ku Hlayisa Misava (Earth Care).
Swi vula ku teka misava, mati, swimilana na swiharhi tani hi “living systems to protect, not resources to use up.”
System leyi u yi tirhisaka yi hela, kutani “stops paying you.” System leyi u yi sirhelelaka ya ya mahlweni, kutani “keeps paying you.”
Languta xiphemu xin'we xa misava leyi nga funengetiwangiki epurasini ra wena. Xana ku na lexi xi yi sirhelelaka sweswi?

sourceBody: The second ethic is People Care.
Your family's needs come first, then your community's.
A farmer who sells every egg and every vegetable, and keeps nothing back for the family table, is skipping People Care.
The farm is meant to feed the household that runs it.
What comes off your land that your own family never eats?
recommendedBody: Nawu wa vumbirhi wa mahanyelo i Ku Hlayisa Vanhu (People Care).
Swilaveko swa ndyangu wa wena swi ta rhanga, ivi swa vaaki va wena swi landzela.
Murimi la xavaka tandza hinkwato ni matsavu hinkwato, kambe a nga hlayisi na xin'we leswaku ndyangu wu ta dya, a nga landzeli People Care.
Purasi ri endleriwe ku phamela swakudya ndyangu lowu wu ri fambisaka.
I yini leswi humaka epurasini ra wena leswi ndyangu wa wena wu nga swi dyiki?

sourceBody: The third ethic is Fair Share.
Take only what you need, and return the surplus to the system — seeds, food, water, knowledge.
A farmer who sells all his surplus mielies and keeps nothing back for compost or for seed is breaking this one. Nothing goes back.
A community that fences off a shared spring is breaking it too.
What does your land get back from you each season?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Ku Avelana hi Ku Ringana (Fair Share)
recommendedBody: Nawu wa vunharhu wa mahanyelo i Ku Avelana hi Ku Ringana (Fair Share).
Teka ntsena leswi u swi lavaka, kutani return the surplus to the system — mbewu, swakudya, mati, vutivi.
Murimi loyi a xaviselaka mielies ya yena leyi saleke yi hundzaka leswi a swi lavaka hinkwaro, a nga hlayisi ni xin’we xa compost kumbe mbewu, u tshova nawu lowu. A ku na lexi tlheleleke.
Vaaki lava va pfangaka xihlovo lexi va xi tirhisaka swin’we hi fence na vona va tshova Fair Share.
Land ya wena yi kuma yini eka wena eka nguva yin’wana ni yin’wana?

sourceBody: A borehole serves your household. Neighbours ask for water too.

First find out if sharing is allowed. Check whether the borehole can serve all users without taking too much. If sharing is allowed and there is enough water, agree how to share fairly and keep watching the water level. People Care and Fair Share guide the agreement. Earth Care means protecting the source. Watching the level alone does not make extra use safe or allowed.
Who could help you check the rules and the water supply?
recommendedBody: A borehole yi tirhela ndyangu wa wena. Vahakelani na vona va kombela mati.

Sungula hi ku kuma leswaku ku avelana swa pfumeleriwa kumbe e-e. Kambela loko borehole yi nga tirhela vatirhisi hinkwavo handle ko teka mati yo tala ngopfu. Loko ku avelana ku pfumeleriwa naswona ku ri na mati yo ringana, pfumelelani ndlela ya ku avelana hi ku ringana, mi ya mahlweni mi languta water level. People Care na Fair Share swi kongomisa ntwanano. Earth Care swi vula ku sirhelela the source. Ku languta water level ntsena a swi endli leswaku ku tirhisa mati yo engetela swi va safe kumbe swi pfumeleriwa.
I mani loyi a nga ku pfuna ku kambela milawu ni mphakelo wa mati?

sourceBody: This is what the ethics are actually for.
A neighbour asks to graze cattle after a drought. A flood damages your swales. Nobody has written down the answer.
The ethics help you weigh the choices and explain your decision. Check the rules and ask permission where it is needed.
Build these three into how you think before you build anything on the ground.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Loko ku nga ri na Buku ya Milawu
recommendedBody: Hi swona leswi milawu ya mahanyelo yi pfunaka swona hakunene.
Muakelani u kombela ku risa tihomu endzhaku ka dyandza. A flood damages your swales. A ku na munhu loyi a tsaleke nhlamulo.
Milawu ya mahanyelo yi ku pfuna ku pima swihlawuriwa ni ku hlamusela xiboho xa wena. Kambela milawu kutani u kombela mpfumelelo laha swi lavekaka kona.
Veka ethics leti tinharhu eka ndlela leyi u ehleketaka ha yona u nga si sungula ku aka ehandle.

sourceBody: David Holmgren set out twelve design principles in Essence of Permaculture. Bill Mollison and David Holmgren co-originated the permaculture concept.
You do not need all twelve to start. Three useful starting points for this lesson are: observe and interact, catch and store energy, and use edges and value the marginal.
We will take those three one at a time.
recommendedBody: David Holmgren u hlamusele twelve design principles eka Essence of Permaculture. Bill Mollison na David Holmgren va sungula permaculture concept swin’we.
A swi lavi ku sungula hi hinkwato ta 12. Kha dyondzo leyi, ku na tindlela tinharhu leti pfunaka ku sungula: observe and interact, catch and store energy, and use edges and value the marginal.
Hi ta teka sweswo swinharhu hi xin'we hi xin'we.

sourceBody: Watch your land through a full season before you commit to major earthworks.
One storm shows you one moment. A full wet season shows you the pattern — where water runs, where it pools, where it never reaches.

This helps you understand the site. It does not by itself show that a swale is suitable or safe to build. Before digging, check the soil, slope, drainage and a safe overflow route that will not cause erosion or send damaging water to neighbours. Ask a trained local adviser to assess the site.
Where does water leave your land? Do you actually know, or are you guessing?
recommendedBody: Languta land ya wena through a full season before you commit to major earthworks.
Storm yin’we yi ku komba nkarhi wun’we. Full wet season yi ku komba pattern: laha mati ya khulukaka, laha ya hlengeletanaka kona, ni laha ma nga fiki kona nikatsongo.

Leswi swi ku pfuna ku twisisa ndhawu. Kambe leswi ntsena a swi kombisi loko swale yi faneleka kumbe yi safe ku akiwa. U nga si cela, kambela soil, slope, drainage na safe overflow route leyi nga ta ka yi nga vangisi erosion kumbe ku rhumela mati lama onhaka eka vaakelani. Kombela trained local adviser a kambela ndhawu.
Xana mati ma huma hi kwihi eka land ya wena? Xana wa swi tiva hakunene kumbe wa bvumbetela?

sourceBody: Harvest rain, sun and biomass before they leave your property.
Every one of those arrives free and leaves free. Water runs off, leaves blow away, sun falls on bare ground.
Compare the cost and work with the benefit on your own farm.
Name one thing that arrives on your land free and leaves again without being used.
recommendedBody: Harvest rain, sun na biomass u nga si swi lahla swi huma eka property ya wena.
Hinkwato swi fika mahala swi tlhela swi famba mahala. Mati ma khuluka ma huma, matluka ma haha ma ya, dyambu ri wela eka bare ground.
Pimanisa  the cost and work with the benefit epurasini ra wena.
Vula xilo xin'we lexi fikaka epurasini ra wena mahala, kutani xi tlhela xi suka xi nga tirhisiwanga.

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Use Edges and Value the Marginal
sourceBody: The edge is where two things meet — a fence line or the strip beside a path.
These can be useful places to observe. Look at what already grows well along yours. That is the land telling you something.
Which edge on your plot is doing nothing at the moment?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Use Edges and Value the Marginal
recommendedBody: The edge hi laha swilo swimbirhi swi hlanganaka kona — a fence line or the strip beside a path.
Leswi swi nga va tindhawu letinene to languta. Languta leswi se swi kulaka kahle etlhelo ka edge ya wena. Yoleyo i land leyi ku byelaka swin’wana.
Hi yihi edge eka plot ya wena leyi nga endli xin’wana sweswi?

sourceBody: Use and value diversity. Hail injury to maize depends on the storm and the crop’s growth stage. This principle does not promise that a crop will survive every event.
Two others worth knowing: produce no waste, so scraps become compost and compost becomes soil. And use small and slow solutions — a bucket can irrigate a bed with no electricity at all.
What would one bad day cost you right now?
recommendedBody: Tirhisa diversity u tlhela u yi teka yi ri ya nkoka. Hail injury to maize depends on the storm and the crop’s growth stage. Principle leyi a yi tiyisisi leswaku crop yi ta pona eka xiendlakalo xin’wana ni xin’wana.

Ku na swin’wana swimbirhi leswi swi nga swinene ku swi tiva: produce no waste, hikokwalaho masalela ma hundzuka compost na compost yi hundzuka misava. Naswona use small and slow solutions — bakiti ri nga cheleta bed handle ka gezi nikatsongo.
Xana siku rin’we ro biha ri nga ku durhela yini sweswi?

sourceBody: Put each element where it works for its neighbours.

A garden, fruit trees and a chicken run arranged so the chickens rotate through the beds after harvest is integration. Keep chickens away from crops being harvested for food. Fresh manure can carry germs. Ask an extension adviser how to manage the bed safely before edible crops return. The chickens can clean up pests and add fertility instead of sitting idle in a fixed pen.
The same three things, fenced apart, do only their own job.
Pick two or three principles that speak to your biggest problem and apply them hard. The rest become obvious as you go.
recommendedBody: Veka element yin’wana ni yin’wana laha yi tirhaka kona na leswi nga ekusuhi na yona.

Ntanga, mirhi ya mihandzu na chicken run swi nga veketeriwa leswaku tihuku ti rotate through the beds after harvest; leswi i integration. U nga pfumeleli tihuku ti tshinela eka crops leti ku tshoveriwaka swakudya. Fresh manure can carry germs. Kombela extension adviser a ku hlamusela ndlela yo hlayisa bed yi ri safe loko edible crops ti nga si tlhela ti byariwa. Tihuku ti nga basisa pests ti tlhela ti engetela fertility, ematshan’weni yo tshama ti nga endli swo karhi eka fixed pen.
Swilo leswi swinharhu, loko swi pfariwe hi fence swi hambanisiwile, xin’wana ni xin’wana xi endla ntirho wa xona ntsena.
Hlawula principles timbirhi kumbe tinharhu leti khumbaka xiphiqo xa wena lexikulu u ti tirhisa swinene. Letin’wana ti ta vonaka kahle loko u ya mahlweni.

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Zones: Organising by How Often You Visit
sourceBody: Zones run from 0 to 5, and they are about your feet, not your fences.
Zone 0 is the house. In this example, Zone 1 is near the house and holds herbs and salad greens picked often.
Zone 2 is the main garden and the chicken run, visited once or twice a day. Zone 3 is the main field, visited weekly.
Zone 4 is semi-wild — fruit trees and fodder that need occasional attention. Zone 5 is left wild.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Zones: Organising by How Often You Visit
recommendedBody: Zones ti suka eka 0 ku ya eka 5, naswona ti khumba ku famba ka wena, ku nga ri ti-fence ta wena.
Zone 0 i yindlu. Eka xifaniso lexi, Zone 1 yi le kusuhi ni yindlu naswona yi na herbs and salad greens leti u ti tshovelaka nkarhi ni nkarhi.
Zone 2 i main garden ni chicken run, u ya eka swona kan’we kumbe kambirhi hi siku. Zone 3 i main field, u ya kona vhiki na vhiki.
Zone 4 i semi-wild: mirhi ya mihandzu na fodder leswi lavaka occasional attention. Zone 5 yi tshikiwa yi ri wild.

sourceBody: Herbs you pick often are easier to tend near the house.
Put them far away, and the long walk may mean you miss a visit. The herbs may be neglected.
Think about the paths you walk each day.
What do you visit often that could be closer?
recommendedBody: Herbs leti u ti tshovelaka nkarhi ni nkarhi swa olova ku ti hlayisa loko ti ri ekusuhi ni yindlu.
Loko u ti veka ekule, riendzo ro leha ri nga endla leswaku u nga ti endzeli. herbs ti nga siyiwa ti nga hlayisiwi.
Ehleketa hi tindlela leti u fambaka eka tona siku rin'wana ni rin'wana.
I yini lexi u xi endzelaka ngopfu lexi a xi fanele ku va ekusuhi?

sourceBody: This is the point of the whole exercise.
Zones help organise space around your effort — the walking, the carrying and the checking that fills a real day.
The more often something needs you, the closer it lives. That can save walking and work over a season.
Stand at your kitchen door. What can you reach without thinking about it?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Zones ti Pulana Ntirho wa Wena
recommendedBody: Hi xona xikongomelo xa ntirho lowu hinkwawo.
Zones ti pfuna ku lulamisa ndhawu hi ku ya hi matshalatshala ya wena — ku famba, ku rhwala ni ku kambela leswi tata siku ra xiviri.
Loko xin’wana xi ku lava nkarhi ni nkarhi, xi tshama ekusuhi na wena. Sweswo swi nga hunguta ku famba ni ku tirha eka nguva.
Yima enyangweni ya khixi. I yini lexi u nga xi fikeleraka handle ko ehleketa?

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Sectors: The Energies Arriving From Outside
sourceBody: Zones come from inside your land. Sectors come from outside it.
Sun, wind, rain, flood and fire all arrive across your boundary whether you plan for them or not.
Watch where strong wind comes from on your farm. Nearby weather-station records can help you check wind direction. Watch where rainwater enters and flows across your land.
Which direction does the weather that damages you come from?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Sectors: The Energies Arriving From Outside
recommendedBody: Zones ti huma endzeni ka land ya wena. Sectors ti huma ehandle ka yona.
Dyambu, moya, mpfula, flood na ndzilo swi tsemakanya ndzilakana wa wena hambi u swi pulanile kumbe a wu swi pulananga.

Languta laha moya wa matimba wu humaka kona epurasini ra wena. Nearby weather-station records ti nga ku pfuna ku kambela wind direction. Languta laha mati ya mpfula ma nghenaka kona ni ndlela leyi ma khulukaka ha yona eka misava ya wena.
Xana maxelo lama ku onhaka ma huma hi tlhelo rihi?

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Watch: Shelter Between Wind and Crops
sourceBody: Look at this example. The wind comes from the north-west.
The trees and shrubs stand between that wind and the crops.
Some air passes through the windbreak. Other air moves over it or around its ends.
The shelter can reduce wind speed behind it. The design and care of the windbreak matter.
On your own site, observe the damaging winds before choosing where to plant. This picture is not a planting plan.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Xiyisisa: Shelter Between Wind and Crops
recommendedBody: Languta example leyi. Moya wu huma hi north-west.
Mirhi na shrubs swi yima exikarhi ka moya wolowo ni crops.
Air yin’wana yi hundza hi le ka windbreak. Other air moves over it or around its ends.
Shelter yi nga hunguta rivilo ra moya endzhaku ka yona. Design ni ku hlayisiwa ka windbreak swi na nkoka.
Eka site ya wena, languta mimoya leyi onhaka u nga si hlawula laha u nga ta byala kona. Picture leyi a hi planting plan.

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Sketch It And You Have A Design
sourceBody: Draw your boundary. Mark the house. Draw the rings outward by how often you visit.
Then draw arrows in from outside for sun, wind, fire and water.
That sheet of paper is the skeleton of your design. Everything else in this course hangs on it.
It does not need to be neat. It needs to be true.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Sketch It And You Have A Design
recommendedBody: Dirowa boundary ya wena. Maka yindlu. Dirowa rings u ya ehandle hi ku ya hi leswaku u endzela ndhawu yin’wana ni yin’wana kangani.
Kutani dirowa miseve leti nghenaka ti huma ehandle ku yimela dyambu, moya, ndzilo na mati.
Phepha leri ri khoma skeleton ya design ya wena. Hinkwaswo swin’wana eka khoso leyi swi titshege hi rona.
A swi bohi leswaku swi va leswi hlelekeke. Swi fanele swi fambisana ni leswi nga kona hakunene.

sourceBody: Sketch your own zones and sectors on one sheet of paper.
Mark Zone 0 and Zone 1 first, then work outward as far as your land goes.
Add an arrow for each energy that arrives from outside, and label where it comes from.
Photograph the sketch.
recommendedBody: Dirowa own zones and sectors eka phepha rin’we.
Maka Zone 0 na Zone 1 ku sungula, kutani u ya ehandle ku fika laha land ya wena yi helelaka kona.
Engetela museve wun’we eka energy yin’wana ni yin’wana leyi fikaka yi huma ehandle, u tsala laha yi humaka kona.
Tekela xifaniso xa sketch ya wena.

sourceBody: Walk out and check your sketch against the ground.
Stand at the kitchen door and count what is really in Zone 1 today.
Find one thing planted further away than how often you use it, and write down where it should move to.
Then ask one older neighbour which direction the worst wind comes from, and compare their answer with your arrow.
recommendedBody: Famba ehandle u kambela sketch ya wena u yi pimanisa ni ground ya xiviri.
Yima enyangweni ya khixi u hlayela leswi nga kona hakunene eka Zone 1 namuntlha.
Kuma xilo xin’we lexi byariweke further away than how often you use it, u tsala laha xi faneleke ku rhurhiseriwa kona.
Endzhaku kombela older neighbour un’we a ku hlamusela direction leyi worst wind yi humaka hi yona, u ringanisa nhlamulo ya yena ni museve wa wena.

sourceBody: Before you dig anything, it helps to know how the decisions get made.
This module is the foundation for everything else in the course. Three ethics, a set of design principles, and one simple way to organise your land.
None of it needs money. All of it changes where you put things, and how far you walk every day.
Think about your own plot. Which part of it do you visit most often?
recommendedBody: Pele o cheka ntho efe kapa efe, ho thusa ho tseba hore na diqeto di etswa jwang.
Thuto ena ke motheo wa tsohle tse ding thutong ena. E na le melao e meraro ya boitshwaro, melao-motheo ya moralo, le mokgwa o le mong o bonolo wa ho hlophisa mobu wa hao.
Ha ho le e nngwe ya dintho tsena e hlokang tjhelete. Tsona kaofela di fetola moo o behang dintho teng le hore o tsamaya sebaka se se kae letsatsi le leng le le leng.
Nahana ka tshimo ya hao. Ke karolo efe ya yona eo o e etelang hangata ho feta tse ding?

sourceBody: A good design saves work before you pick up a spade.
Most of the effort on a smallholding is not planting or harvesting. It is walking, carrying and fixing what was put in the wrong place.
Permaculture is a way of deciding where things go, so the land works with you instead of against you.
Think of one job on your farm that takes longer than it should. Where does the time actually go?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Lebaka Leo Sena se Leng Bohlokwa ka Lona
recommendedBody: Moralo o motle o fokotsa mosebetsi pele o nka garawe.
Mosebetsi o mongata polasing e nyenyane ha se ho lema kapa ho kotula. Ke ho tsamaya, ho rwala le ho lokisa se neng se behilwe sebakeng se fosahetseng.
Permaculture ke mokgwa wa ho etsa qeto ya hore dintho di be hokae, e le hore mobu o sebetse mmoho le wena ho e-na le ho o sitisa.
Nahana ka mosebetsi o le mong polasing ya hao o nkang nako e telele ho feta kamoo o lokelang. Nako eo e ya hokae?

sourceBody: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things.
Name the three ethics, and use them to settle a decision that has no obvious answer.
Name the design principles that matter most on your land, and say why.
Sketch your zones and your sectors on one sheet of paper.
That sketch is the skeleton of every plan you make after this.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Dintho Tseo o Tla Kgona ho di Etsa
recommendedBody: Qetellong ya thuto ena o tla kgona ho etsa dintho tse tharo.
Bolela melao e meraro ya boitshwaro, mme o e sebedise ho rarolla qeto e se nang karabo e totobetseng.
Bolela melao-motheo ya moralo e leng bohlokwa haholo mobung wa hao, mme o bolele lebaka.
Rala zones le sectors tsa hao pampiring e le nngwe.
Setshwantsho seo ke motheo wa moralo o mong le o mong oo o tla o etsa kamora moo.

sourceBody: The first ethic is Earth Care.
It means treating soil, water, plants and animals as living systems to protect, not resources to use up.
A system you use up stops paying you. A system you protect keeps paying you.
Look at one patch of bare soil on your land. Is anything protecting it right now?
recommendedBody: Molao wa pele wa boitshwaro ke Tlhokomelo ya Lefatshe (Earth Care).
Ho bolela ho nka mobu, metsi, dimela le diphoofolo e le ditsamaiso tse phelang tse lokelang ho sireletswa, eseng mehlodi eo re ka e sebedisang ho fihlela e fela.
Sheba karolo e le nngwe ya mobu o se nang dimela tshimong ya hao. Na ho na le ntho e o sireletsang hona jwale?

sourceBody: The second ethic is People Care.
Your family's needs come first, then your community's.
A farmer who sells every egg and every vegetable, and keeps nothing back for the family table, is skipping People Care.
The farm is meant to feed the household that runs it.
What comes off your land that your own family never eats?
recommendedBody: Molao wa bobedi wa boitshwaro ke Tlhokomelo ya Batho (People Care).
Ditlhoko tsa lelapa la hao di tla pele, ebe ho latela tsa setjhaba sa heno.
Polasi e reretswe ho fepa lelapa le e tsamaisang.
Ke eng e tswang mobung wa hao eo lelapa la hao le sa e jeng?

sourceBody: The third ethic is Fair Share.
Take only what you need, and return the surplus to the system — seeds, food, water, knowledge.
A farmer who sells all his surplus mielies and keeps nothing back for compost or for seed is breaking this one. Nothing goes back.
A community that fences off a shared spring is breaking it too.
What does your land get back from you each season?
recommendedBody: Molao wa boraro wa boitshwaro ke Karolelano e Lokileng (Fair Share).
Mobu wa hao o fumana eng ho wena sehleng ka seng?

sourceBody: A borehole serves your household. Neighbours ask for water too.

First find out if sharing is allowed. Check whether the borehole can serve all users without taking too much. If sharing is allowed and there is enough water, agree how to share fairly and keep watching the water level. People Care and Fair Share guide the agreement. Earth Care means protecting the source. Watching the level alone does not make extra use safe or allowed.
Who could help you check the rules and the water supply?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Shebella: Qeto e le Nngwe, Melao e Meraro ya Boitshwaro
recommendedBody: Ke mang ya ka o thusang ho sheba melao le phepelo ya metsi?

sourceBody: This is what the ethics are actually for.
A neighbour asks to graze cattle after a drought. A flood damages your swales. Nobody has written down the answer.
The ethics help you weigh the choices and explain your decision. Check the rules and ask permission where it is needed.
Build these three into how you think before you build anything on the ground.
recommendedBody: Ke ka lebaka lena melao ya boitshwaro e leng teng.

sourceBody: David Holmgren set out twelve design principles in Essence of Permaculture. Bill Mollison and David Holmgren co-originated the permaculture concept.
You do not need all twelve to start. Three useful starting points for this lesson are: observe and interact, catch and store energy, and use edges and value the marginal.
We will take those three one at a time.
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Melao-motheo e Leshome le Metso e Mmedi
recommendedBody: David Holmgren o hlalositse melao-motheo e leshome le metso e mmedi ya moralo bukeng ya *Essence of Permaculture*. Bill Mollison le David Holmgren ba thehile mohopolo wa permaculture mmoho.
Re tla bua ka e nngwe le e nngwe ya melao-motheo eo e meraro ka bonngwe.

sourceBody: Watch your land through a full season before you commit to major earthworks.
One storm shows you one moment. A full wet season shows you the pattern — where water runs, where it pools, where it never reaches.

This helps you understand the site. It does not by itself show that a swale is suitable or safe to build. Before digging, check the soil, slope, drainage and a safe overflow route that will not cause erosion or send damaging water to neighbours. Ask a trained local adviser to assess the site.
Where does water leave your land? Do you actually know, or are you guessing?
Harvest rain, sun and biomass before they leave your property.
Every one of those arrives free and leaves free. Water runs off, leaves blow away, sun falls on bare ground.
Compare the cost and work with the benefit on your own farm.
Name one thing that arrives on your land free and leaves again without being used.
recommendedBody: E nngwe le e nngwe ya tsona e fihla e sa lefellwe mme e tsamaya e sa lefellwe. Metsi a phalla a tloha, makgasi a fefolwa ke moya, letsatsi le kganyetsa mobu o se nang dimela.
Bolela ntho e le nngwe e fihlang mobung wa hao e sa lefellwe, ebe e boela e tsamaya e sa sebediswa.

fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.sourceHeading: Use Edges and Value the Marginal
sourceBody: The edge is where two things meet — a fence line or the strip beside a path.
These can be useful places to observe. Look at what already grows well along yours. That is the land telling you something.
Which edge on your plot is doing nothing at the moment?
fullRecommendedBodyCompositions.recommendedHeading: Use Edges and Value the Marginal
recommendedBody: Moeli ke moo lintho tse peli li kopanang teng — joalo ka mola oa terata kapa sebaka se pela tsela.
Libaka tsena li ka ba molemo bakeng sa ho shebella. Sheba hore na ke eng e seng e mela hantle pela moeli oa hao. Seo ke tsela eo mobu o u bolellang ho hong ka eona.
Ke karolo efe ea moeli setšeng sa hao e sa etse letho hona joale?

sourceBody: Use and value diversity. Hail injury to maize depends on the storm and the crop’s growth stage. This principle does not promise that a crop will survive every event.
Two others worth knowing: produce no waste, so scraps become compost and compost becomes soil. And use small and slow solutions — a bucket can irrigate a bed with no electricity at all.
What would one bad day cost you right now?
Put each element where it works for its neighbours.

A garden, fruit trees and a chicken run arranged so the chickens rotate through the beds after harvest is integration. Keep chickens away from crops being harvested for food. Fresh manure can carry germs. Ask an extension adviser how to manage the bed safely before edible crops return. The chickens can clean up pests and add fertility instead of sitting idle in a fixed pen.
The same three things, fenced apart, do only their own job.
Pick two or three principles that speak to your biggest problem and apply them hard. The rest become obvious as you go.

body: The first ethic is Earth Care.
It means treating soil, water, plants and animals as living systems to protect, not resources to use up.

Your family's needs come first, then your community's.

Take only what you need, and return the surplus to the system — seeds, food, water, knowledge.

body: Watch your land through a full season before you commit to major earthworks.

body: Put each element where it works for its neighbours.

The chickens can clean up pests and add fertility instead of sitting idle in a fixed pen.
The same three things, fenced apart, do only their own job.

body: The first ethic is Earth Care.
It means treating soil, water, plants and animals as living systems to protect, not resources to use up.

english.heading: Integrate Rather Than Segregate
body: Put each element where it works for its neighbours.

A garden, fruit trees and a chicken run arranged so the chickens rotate through the beds after harvest is integration. Keep chickens away from crops being harvested for food. Fresh manure can carry germs. Ask an extension adviser how to manage the bed safely before edible crops return. The chickens can clean up pests and add fertility instead of sitting idle in a fixed pen.
The same three things, fenced apart, do only their own job.

english.heading: Introduction to Permaculture
body: Before you dig anything, it helps to know how the decisions get made.
This module is the foundation for everything else in the course. Three ethics, a set of design principles, and one simple way to organise your land.
None of it needs money. All of it changes where you put things, and how far you walk every day.
Think about your own plot. Which part of it do you visit most often?

heading.text: Selelekela sa Permaculture

body.text: Pele o cheka ntho efe kapa efe, ho thusa ho tseba hore na diqeto di etswa jwang.
Thuto ena ke motheo wa tsohle tse ding thutong ena. E na le melao e meraro ya boitshwaro, melao-motheo ya moralo, le mokgwa o le mong o bonolo wa ho hlophisa mobu wa hao.
Ha ho le e nngwe ya dintho tsena e hlokang tjhelete. Tsona kaofela di fetola moo o behang dintho teng le hore o tsamaya sebaka se se kae letsatsi le leng le le leng.
Nahana ka tshimo ya hao. Ke karolo efe ya yona eo o e etelang hangata ho feta tse ding?

english.heading: Why This Matters
body: A good design saves work before you pick up a spade.
Most of the effort on a smallholding is not planting or harvesting. It is walking, carrying and fixing what was put in the wrong place.
Permaculture is a way of deciding where things go, so the land works with you instead of against you.
Think of one job on your farm that takes longer than it should. Where does the time actually go?

heading.text: Lebaka Leo Sena se Leng Bohlokwa ka Lona

body.text: Moralo o motle o fokotsa mosebetsi pele o nka garawe.
Mosebetsi o mongata polasing e nyenyane ha se ho lema kapa ho kotula. Ke ho tsamaya, ho rwala le ho lokisa se neng se behilwe sebakeng se fosahetseng.
Permaculture ke mokgwa wa ho etsa qeto ya hore dintho di be hokae, e le hore mobu o sebetse mmoho le wena ho e-na le ho o sitisa.
Nahana ka mosebetsi o le mong polasing ya hao o nkang nako e telele ho feta kamoo o lokelang. Nako eo e ya hokae?

english.heading: Learning Outcomes
body: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things.
Name the three ethics, and use them to settle a decision that has no obvious answer.
Name the design principles that matter most on your land, and say why.
Sketch your zones and your sectors on one sheet of paper.
That sketch is the skeleton of every plan you make after this.

heading.text: Dintho Tseo o Tla Kgona ho di Etsa

body.text: Qetellong ya thuto ena o tla kgona ho etsa dintho tse tharo.
Bolela melao e meraro ya boitshwaro, mme o e sebedise ho rarolla qeto e se nang karabo e totobetseng.
Bolela melao-motheo ya moralo e leng bohlokwa haholo mobung wa hao, mme o bolele lebaka.
Rala zones le sectors tsa hao pampiring e le nngwe.
Setshwantsho seo ke motheo wa moralo o mong le o mong oo o tla o etsa kamora moo.

english.heading: Earth Care
body: The first ethic is Earth Care.
It means treating soil, water, plants and animals as living systems to protect, not resources to use up.
A system you use up stops paying you. A system you protect keeps paying you.
Look at one patch of bare soil on your land. Is anything protecting it right now?

heading.text: Tlhokomelo ya Lefatshe

body.text: Molao wa pele wa boitshwaro ke Tlhokomelo ya Lefatshe (Earth Care).
Ho bolela ho nka mobu, metsi, dimela le diphoofolo e le ditsamaiso tse phelang tse lokelang ho sireletswa, eseng mehlodi eo re ka e sebedisang ho fihlela e fela.
Sheba karolo e le nngwe ya mobu o se nang dimela tshimong ya hao. Na ho na le ntho e o sireletsang hona jwale?

english.heading: People Care
body: The second ethic is People Care.
Your family's needs come first, then your community's.
A farmer who sells every egg and every vegetable, and keeps nothing back for the family table, is skipping People Care.
The farm is meant to feed the household that runs it.
What comes off your land that your own family never eats?

heading.text: Tlhokomelo ya Batho

body.text: Molao wa bobedi wa boitshwaro ke Tlhokomelo ya Batho (People Care).
Ditlhoko tsa lelapa la hao di tla pele, ebe ho latela tsa setjhaba sa heno.
Polasi e reretswe ho fepa lelapa le e tsamaisang.
Ke eng e tswang mobung wa hao eo lelapa la hao le sa e jeng?

english.heading: Fair Share
body: The third ethic is Fair Share.
Take only what you need, and return the surplus to the system — seeds, food, water, knowledge.
A farmer who sells all his surplus mielies and keeps nothing back for compost or for seed is breaking this one. Nothing goes back.
A community that fences off a shared spring is breaking it too.
What does your land get back from you each season?

heading.text: Karolelano e Lokileng (Fair Share)

body.text: Molao wa boraro wa boitshwaro ke Karolelano e Lokileng (Fair Share).

english.heading: Watch: One Decision, Three Ethics
body: A borehole serves your household. Neighbours ask for water too.

First find out if sharing is allowed. Check whether the borehole can serve all users without taking too much. If sharing is allowed and there is enough water, agree how to share fairly and keep watching the water level. People Care and Fair Share guide the agreement. Earth Care means protecting the source. Watching the level alone does not make extra use safe or allowed.

body: This is what the ethics are actually for.
A neighbour asks to graze cattle after a drought. A flood damages your swales. Nobody has written down the answer.
The ethics help you weigh the choices and explain your decision. Check the rules and ask permission where it is needed.
Build these three into how you think before you build anything on the ground.

english.heading: Twelve Principles
body: David Holmgren set out twelve design principles in Essence of Permaculture. Bill Mollison and David Holmgren co-originated the permaculture concept.
You do not need all twelve to start. Three useful starting points for this lesson are: observe and interact, catch and store energy, and use edges and value the marginal.
We will take those three one at a time.

Re tla bua ka e nngwe le e nngwe ya melao-motheo eo e meraro ka bonngwe.

english.heading: Observe and Interact
body: Watch your land through a full season before you commit to major earthworks.
One storm shows you one moment. A full wet season shows you the pattern — where water runs, where it pools, where it never reaches.

This helps you understand the site. It does not by itself show that a swale is suitable or safe to build. Before digging, check the soil, slope, drainage and a safe overflow route that will not cause erosion or send damaging water to neighbours. Ask a trained local adviser to assess the site.

english.heading: Catch and Store Energy
body: Harvest rain, sun and biomass before they leave your property.
Every one of those arrives free and leaves free. Water runs off, leaves blow away, sun falls on bare ground.
Compare the cost and work with the benefit on your own farm.
Name one thing that arrives on your land free and leaves again without being used.
